work_completed: I reproduced the reds first (6 failed, 26 passed). The cause was a false positive. The test copies nothing: it only runs `git log` and `git status` on named paths. But its skip call `pytest.skip(f"{S.REPO_ROOT} is not a git worktree")` names the repository root and contains the words "git worktree". W1-28's check (`tests/acceptance/W1-28/w1_28_copy_check.py:165`, `_SHELL_ROUTE`) reads that as a whole-tree route. A fresh test designer, sandboxed at effort high in the `W2-108-tests` worktree, changed only the message of that skip, with `Rewrite-Reason: DEC-385 (DEC-977)`. The skip condition, the paths and both git assertions are unchanged, so nothing is weakened. I merged its branch with `--no-ff` and a message file, ran the named suites alone to their end, wrote a `gov checkpoint` record and committed it, and removed the tests worktree and its branch.

discoveries: W1-28's whole-tree check searches every string constant in a call that names the root, message text included (`w1_28_copy_check.py:165`). Any `pytest.skip`, `pytest.fail` or assert message that puts `REPO_ROOT` next to "git worktree", "git clone", "rsync", "cp -r" or "tar c…" is flagged as a whole-tree copy. No list rows: the ticket's `list_rows` is empty.
risks: A later edit that puts a route's words back next to the root in any acceptance test's message turns W1-28 and W1-50 red again. The check's own message makes that quick to diagnose.
lessons: Keep `REPO_ROOT` out of messages that contain git, rsync, tar or cp route words until W1-28's check ignores message text. Inside the sandbox, `git status` lists placeholder dotfiles (character devices); the tracked tree is clean.
